result: The study analyzed 1061 serum samples from 925 individuals (535 lung cancer cases and 263 controls from 645 smokers) using RNA sequencing with 18 million reads per sample. After quality control and filtering, 3306 RNA features across multiple classes (miRNAs, isomiRs, miscRNAs, piRNAs, tRFs, mRNAs, lncRNAs) were selected for modeling. Cases and controls were matched on confounders including age, sex, and blood donor group.
evaluation: The sample collection, processing, and quality control procedures are clearly described with specific numbers (C2, C40, C42). The RNA sequencing methodology (C3, C194), bioinformatics pipeline (C195-C202), and matching strategy (C203-C205) are well-documented. The study design appropriately controls for known confounders.

result: Five machine learning algorithms (lasso, elastic-net, SGL, RF, XGBoost) were evaluated using a rigorous workflow with 70/30 train/test splits repeated five times. XGBoost achieved the best performance with AUC of 0.71 (95% CI, 0.68-0.73) for all histologies, outperforming the average AUC of 0.67 across all algorithms. All algorithms showed consistent acceptable performance despite varying model complexity (RF selected >3000 features vs. lasso <25 features).
evaluation: The ML workflow is methodologically sound with proper train/test splitting (C216-C217), five-fold cross-validation (C218), and repeated evaluation (C36, C217). Performance metrics are reported with confidence intervals (C49-C53, C220-C222). The comparison across algorithms is fair and XGBoost's superiority is clearly demonstrated (C52, C57).

result: Machine learning models using serum RNA levels can robustly separate smokers who will be diagnosed with lung cancer within 10 years from healthy controls regardless of histology, achieving an average AUC of 0.76 (95% CI, 0.68-0.83). This demonstrates that lung cancer can be detected years before diagnosis and symptom manifestation.
evaluation: The claim is supported by the frequent feature model results (C4, C94) tested on independent leave-out datasets including both smokers and non-smokers. The AUC of 0.76 with tight confidence intervals indicates clinically relevant performance. The 10-year prediagnostic window is substantiated by the study design (C185) and time-stratified analyses (C82-C102).

result: Time-stratified and histology-specific models achieved superior performance: NSCLC models predicted cancer 6-8 years before diagnosis with AUC 0.82 (95% CI, 0.76-0.88), while SCLC models predicted cancer 2-5 years before diagnosis with AUC 0.89 (95% CI, 0.77-1.0). The best prediagnostic models reached AUCs up to 0.9, demonstrating that incorporating temporal dynamics and histology improves prediction accuracy.
evaluation: The time-stratified modeling approach is well-justified by prior work showing dynamic RNA levels (C81, C136). The reported AUCs for specific time windows (C5, C6, C83, C88, C101, C102) are supported by the sliding window methodology (C224-C226). The consistency of important features across related models (C85) strengthens confidence in the findings.

result: The most important RNA separators were microRNAs, miscellaneous RNAs, isomiRs, and tRNA-derived fragments. Single RNA class models showed that miscRNA-only and miRNA-only models achieved better performance than other RNA classes. Top features included specific miRNAs (hsa-miR-486-5p, hsa-miR-30a-5p), isomiRs, piRNAs (piR-hsa-28723), and miscRNAs (RN7SL181P, Y-RNA).
evaluation: The identification of important RNA classes is supported by systematic single-class modeling (C67, C69) and feature importance analysis across multiple algorithms (C56, C61, C62). The consistency of top features across different algorithms (C61, C62) and models (C58-C60) strengthens the findings. The biological relevance of many identified features is validated by literature (C116-C138).

result: KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of important RNA features identified significant enrichment (p<0.01) of cancer-related pathways including MAPK, PI3K-Akt, RAS, mTOR, AMPK signaling, and choline metabolism. The enrichment of choline metabolism pathway years before diagnosis (NSCLC 6-8 years, SCLC 2-5 years) supports previous findings that choline-containing phospholipids are potential lung cancer biomarkers.
evaluation: The pathway enrichment analysis is methodologically sound using established tools (C206) and appropriate target prediction databases (C207). The identification of cancer-related pathways (C63, C87, C90, C140) is biologically plausible and consistent with known cancer biology. The choline metabolism findings (C141, C144) are corroborated by independent literature (C142, C143, C145).

result: Feature selection methods (lasso, univariate significance, single RNA class) improved model performance and reduced complexity. Lasso selection improved AUC values while reducing features to ~50-150 RNAs. Univariate significance selection greatly reduced complexity (SCLC models to only 11 RNAs) while maintaining acceptable performance.
evaluation: The feature selection approaches are clearly described (C229-C232) and systematically evaluated (C72, C76). The improvements in both performance and model simplicity are documented with specific metrics (Table 2, C72, C76). The identification of consistent important features across selection methods (C73-C75, C78-C80) strengthens confidence in the biomarker candidates.

result: Frequent feature models compiled from the most important features achieved improved performance: AUC 0.76 (0.68-0.83) for all histologies, 0.78 (0.70-0.85) for NSCLC, and 0.88 (0.83-0.94) for SCLC in smokers. Smokers with positive tests had more than 2-fold increased risk of lung cancer diagnosis. SCLC models maintained high performance (AUC 0.84) even when including non-smokers.
evaluation: The frequent feature models were properly validated using leave-out datasets never used in training (C236, C163). The relative risk calculations are appropriately performed (C238-C240) and clinically meaningful (C100, C153). The robustness of SCLC models to non-smoker inclusion (C99) is notable, though limited by small non-smoker case numbers (C43, C169).

result: Using one sample per patient versus all samples from the same individuals produced comparable model performance for all histologies and NSCLC, though SCLC models performed slightly worse, likely due to smaller sample size. This analysis addressed potential overfitting concerns from using multiple samples per individual.
evaluation: The sensitivity analysis directly addresses a potential methodological concern (C158) and demonstrates robustness of the main findings (C64, C159). The explanation for SCLC performance difference is reasonable given the smaller sample size (C66). This strengthens confidence that the reported results are not artifacts of the sampling strategy.

result: Many identified important features have established biological relevance to cancer: hsa-miR-30a-5p is a tumor suppressor downregulated in LC tissues; hsa-miR-574-5p promotes NSCLC metastasis and was previously proposed as a biomarker; hsa-miR-486-5p targets PIK3R1 and was proposed as a diagnostic/prognostic NSCLC biomarker; 7SL binds TP53 mRNA and downregulates its expression; Y-RNA-derived small RNAs function as tumor suppressors in NSCLC.
evaluation: The biological validation of identified features through literature is comprehensive and well-cited (C117-C138). The consistency between the study's findings and prior knowledge strengthens confidence in the biomarker candidates. However, this represents validation of known associations rather than novel biological discoveries.

result: Two temporal modeling approaches were compared: sliding windows (2, 3, 4-year windows moved across 10 years) and fixed windows (0-2, 0-5, 0-8 years before diagnosis). Sliding window models performed better on specific time intervals, while fixed window models showed only slight improvement over full-time models.
evaluation: Both approaches are clearly described (C224-C227) and systematically compared (C91, C92). The finding that sliding windows outperform fixed windows for specific intervals is consistent with the dynamic nature of prediagnostic RNA levels (C81, C136). This methodological comparison strengthens the rationale for time-stratified modeling.

result: Study strengths include: large prediagnostic sample size with controls from the same cohort, detailed clinical information from cancer registry and surveys, control for confounders (age, sex, blood donor group), consistency with current literature for known biomarkers, and discovery of potential biomarkers from overlooked RNA classes. The study is unique in including samples up to 10 years prior to diagnosis.
evaluation: The stated strengths are well-supported by the study design and execution (C146-C148). The consistency with literature (C149) and novelty of findings (C150) are appropriately balanced. The uniqueness claim (C108) is justified by the 10-year prediagnostic window and large sample size.

result: Study limitations include: lack of independent cohort validation (addressed by training-testing repeats), potential overfitting from feature selection methods and frequent feature models (addressed by leave-out datasets), focus on smokers (though acceptable performance shown for non-smokers), and potential RNA degradation in long-term storage (shown to be negligible and controlled by matching). Insufficient non-smoker cases limit validation of biomarker performance in this population.
evaluation: The authors transparently acknowledge limitations (C154, C157, C158, C160, C162, C164) and describe mitigation strategies (C156, C159, C163, C165, C166). The limitation regarding non-smoker validation (C169) is appropriately acknowledged. The honest assessment of weaknesses and attempts to address them strengthen the overall credibility of the work.

result: The authors propose that serum RNAs can be promising prediagnostic biomarkers for lung cancer screening, from early detection to risk assessment. They suggest a clinical model where full-time models assess initial risk in smokers, followed by biennial testing with prediagnostic models for elevated-risk individuals to confirm preneoplasia or early-stage tumors and guide CT monitoring. Top models achieving AUCs up to 0.9 suggest great potential for early prediction.
evaluation: While the model performance data support potential clinical utility (C104, C182), the proposed clinical implementation framework (C172-C174, C176) is largely speculative and requires prospective validation in screening programs (C179). The claim about preventing unnecessary LDCT use (C178) is not directly tested. The high specificity of prediagnostic models (C175) is promising but determining histology before diagnosis (C176) requires further research (C177).
